original_value: AbstractIdentification of structural parameters for large structures is challenging due to the large number of unknowns and its possibly ill‐conditioned nature. Substructure identification provides a feasible solution to partition a structure into substructures to tackle these difficulties and it has received considerable attention in the recent decades. Although there are variants of substructure identification methods, they share the key to back‐calculate the boundary force of the substructure using response measurements. It will then be treated as part of the input to the substructure. However, one major drawback is the deterioration of the identifiability of the inverse problem due to the reduction of effective constraints and the complicated interdependence relationship between the model parameters and the boundary force. In this article, an improved Bayesian substructure identification approach is proposed without the requirement of input or boundary force measurements. The crux is to model the boundary force as filtered white noise because it is an internal response of the system. This provides extra constraints to enhance the identifiability of the inverse problem. Furthermore, the proposed approach provides not only the most probable values of the identified parameters but also their associated uncertainties. This is an important indicator of identifiability, especially for this case. Examples of a 100‐story building are presented to demonstrate the proposed method. Comparison is also presented to confirm that the proposed method resolves the ill‐conditioned problem encountered in absolute acceleration measurements using existing methods.

result.paraphrase: Structural parameter identification for large structures is difficult because of the many unknown variables and the potential for ill-conditioning. Substructure identification offers a practical way to divide a structure into smaller substructures to address these challenges, and it has attracted substantial attention in recent decades. While substructure identification methods vary, they all rely on back-calculating the substructure boundary force from response measurements, which is then treated as an input to the substructure. A key limitation is that identifiability of the inverse problem deteriorates because effective constraints are reduced and because model parameters and boundary force are strongly interdependent. This article proposes an improved Bayesian substructure identification method that does not require input or boundary force measurements. Its key idea is to represent the boundary force as filtered white noise, since it is an internal system response; this adds constraints and improves inverse-problem identifiability. In addition, the proposed method yields not only the most likely parameter values but also their associated uncertainties, an important identifiability indicator in this setting. A 100-story building example is used to demonstrate the method, and a comparison is provided to show that it overcomes the ill-conditioned problem associated with absolute acceleration measurements in existing methods.
